title: What Happens When You Type a URL
description: Follow a single keystroke from your browser to a server and back — discovering DNS, TCP, and HTTP along the way.

segments.text: Every time you type a URL and hit Enter, an incredible chain of events fires off in milliseconds. Today, we're going to follow that journey step by step.
You type 'www.example.com' into your browser. Simple, right? But your computer has no idea where 'example.com' actually lives. It needs an address — like needing a street address, not just a name.
So how does your computer turn a human-friendly name into a machine-friendly address? Think of it like calling directory assistance to get a phone number.
segments.thought_prompt: How do you think your computer finds the IP address for a domain name?

segments.text: That's DNS — the Domain Name System. Your browser asks a DNS resolver: 'Hey, what's the IP address for example.com?' The resolver checks its cache, or asks root servers, and returns something like 93.184.216.34.

Now your browser knows where to go. But before sending any data, it needs to establish a reliable connection. This is the TCP three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Think of it as a polite introduction before a conversation.
Connection established! Your browser now sends an HTTP request: 'GET /index.html'. It's like placing an order at a restaurant — you specify exactly what you want, and the kitchen gets to work.
The server receives your request, processes it — maybe querying a database, running some logic — and assembles the response. This all happens in milliseconds on a good day.

The server sends back an HTTP response with a status code — 200 means 'here you go!', 404 means 'I can't find that', 500 means 'something broke on my end'. Along with it comes the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
Here's something to think about. All of this — DNS, TCP handshake, HTTP request, server processing, and response — usually happens in under 200 milliseconds.
segments.thought_prompt: Why do you think some websites feel slow if all this happens in under 200ms?

segments.text: Finally, your browser parses the HTML, fetches additional resources like images and scripts, builds the DOM tree, applies CSS styles, and paints pixels on your screen. The page appears!

So a single URL press triggers: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, HTTP request, server processing, HTTP response, and browser rendering. Each layer builds on the one before it, like a perfectly choreographed relay race.

Understanding this flow is foundational. Every system design conversation assumes you know how data travels across the internet. Next, we'll dig deeper into each of these layers and see where things can go wrong — and how to fix them.
